clue.text: He had his day in the Forsyth saga

definitions.text: He had his day in the Forsyth saga

parts.words: He had his day in the Forsyth saga
parts.note: Frederick Forsyth's thriller is titled The Day of the ..., after its assassin's code name, so this figure had his Day in that story

explanation.definitionFit: The assassin in Forsyth's novel The Day of the Jackal goes by this animal's name as a code name.

clue.text: Marine snake beginning to, tip vessel

parts.note: Jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine
a boa is a large constricting snake

indicators.note: the beginning of the word tip means just its first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A sea serpent starts to capsize a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: JOLLY is old Royal Navy slang for a Royal Marine; 'beginning to' picks the first letter of 'tip'.
explanation.definitionFit: A jolly boat is a small ship's boat, a kind of vessel used for ferrying crew.

clue.text: Fish put in order in Scotland and cleaned

parts.note: char is a trout-like freshwater fish
red (or redd) is a Scots verb meaning to tidy up, past tense the same

explanation.surface: A fish is laid out neatly north of the border and gutted.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the verb 'char', to do housework as a charwoman does, whose past tense is spelt the same as 'burnt'. RED or REDD is Scots for tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: To char is to clean houses for pay, so charred means did the cleaning.

clue.text: Soft? No, hard-boiled, etc.

indicators.note: boiled suggests cooking that churns things about, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A breakfast debate about eggs: not soft but hard-boiled, and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard-boiled' looks like one egg word, but 'hard' is fodder and 'boiled' the anagram signal over SOFT, NO and HARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Etc., short for et cetera, is the Latin for continuing a list in the same way.

clue.text: Eponymous hero entangled, not quite entrapped

indicators.note: entangled means the letters are knotted into a new order
not quite the whole word, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A title character gets caught up, almost trapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims the D from 'entrapped', and 'entangled' rearranges the remaining ENTRAPPE.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's play and book are named after their boy hero, so he is the eponymous one.

clue.text: Laid-back midshipman in action

parts.note: Mr Midshipman Easy is the hero of Captain Marryat's naval novel
going means working or in operation

explanation.surface: A relaxed young naval officer on duty.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Midshipman Easy is an 1836 novel by Frederick Marryat; its hero gives EASY.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone relaxed and tolerant is described as easy-going, a synonym.

clue.text: With match, over, a number brought in leave

indicators.note: brought in means the number is placed inside the other piece
over signals the word for the match is turned round

parts.note: a tie is a match between teams in a cup
X is the Roman numeral ten

explanation.surface: A football tie ends and someone is told to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns TIE into EIT; 'brought in' puts X (Roman ten) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Exit as a verb means to go out, a synonym of depart.

clue.text: Father love welcomed by model baby

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: welcomed by means taken inside the following piece

parts.note: to pose is to model for an artist
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Dad's affection is greeted by a fashion model with a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcomed by' puts O (love, zero in tennis) inside POSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A papoose is a Native American infant carried on the back, hence a baby.

clue.text: From Bergen or Senja, possibly

indicators.note: from means the letters are taken out of the run of clue words that follows

explanation.surface: Something comes from one Norwegian place or another.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'Bergen', 'or' and the start of 'Senja'; Bergen and Senja are both in Norway, so the whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse means Norwegian, and Bergen is a city and Senja an island in Norway.

clue.text: Hence giant is overthrown

indicators.note: overthrown means turned upside down, so in a down clue the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: an ogre is a man-eating giant of folk tales

explanation.surface: Therefore the giant has been toppled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergo is Latin for therefore, used to mean consequently.

clue.text: Duck leaves shrub to become a swimmer

indicators.note: leaves means goes away from, so that letter is removed

parts.note: oleander is an evergreen flowering shrub
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: A duck abandons a bush and takes to the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is O, a nil score in cricket. 'leaves' looks like foliage on the shrub but is the removal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Leander swam the Hellespont each night to meet Hero.

clue.text: Garment, a light shoe

parts.note: a slip is a woman's undergarment
a as in so much a head means per

explanation.surface: A list of clothing: an item, and some footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' gives PER, as in 'ten pounds a head'.
explanation.definitionFit: A slipper is a soft, light indoor shoe.

clue.text: The hand out of honours

parts.note: in whist or bridge, a dealt hand holding no card above a nine, so none of the honour cards

explanation.surface: Sounds like the distribution of a New Year's list of awards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hand out of honours' suggests giving out awards; it is a card hand lacking honour cards, named after an Earl of Yarborough who offered odds against it.
explanation.definitionFit: In whist or bridge this term names a hand with no card higher than nine.

clue.text: Nobody is religious, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: a religious, as a noun, is a monk or nun

explanation.surface: A person claims nobody is devout, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'religious' is a noun here: a member of a religious order, NUN.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun means not one person, a synonym of no one.

clue.text: They require a trichologist to be pernickety

explanation.definitionFit: Hairs that have split ends call for a hair specialist; quibbling over tiny distinctions is the idiom for being fussy.

clue.text: A rhyme for yellow

parts.note: a dull yellow shade whose two-word name is itself a rhyme, the first word chiming with the second

explanation.definitionFit: The colour name is a dull brownish-yellow shade, and its two words rhyme.

clue.text: An unknown nightmare?

parts.note: read the word nightmare as a mare of the night, a horse of darkness, and the phrase is an unknown contender

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a competitor whose ability is unknown, and a night mare would be a horse in the dark.

clue.text: Simpers foolishly, to produce an effect

indicators.note: foolishly suggests silly behaviour, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone simpers in a silly way to make an impression.
explanation.definitionFit: To impress is to leave a strong mark on someone, to make an impact.

clue.text: A hitch, and he'd be sent bonkers

indicators.note: bonkers is British slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: A snag, and the man would be driven mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hitch' is a knot, not a snag; 'bonkers' (British slang for mad) rearranges HEDBESENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheet bend is a sailor's knot for joining two ropes, a kind of hitch.

clue.text: Soldiers chasing characteristic deserter

parts.note: a trait is a distinguishing characteristic
OR is short for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Troops pursue a typical runaway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chasing' means coming after, so the soldiers go last. OR stands for other ranks, enlisted soldiers who are not officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A traitor abandons his cause or side, as a deserter does.

clue.text: A reason for being stranded

parts.note: grounds are reasons, as in grounds for complaint

explanation.surface: A justification for being left high and dry.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship aground is stuck on the bottom, stranded in shallow water.

clue.text: What's used to cook scones? Key question!

parts.note: G is a musical key
a riddle is a puzzling question

explanation.surface: A baker asks what pan to use for scones, the vital question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key question' looks like 'the main question'; it is G, a musical key, then RIDDLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A griddle is a flat iron plate for cooking girdle scones and pancakes.

clue.text: Let down and fed up, departed

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: late means dead, departed this life

explanation.surface: Disappointed and fed up, someone leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed up' looks like a phrase meaning bored; 'up' turns FED into DEF. LATE means departed, as in the late king.
explanation.definitionFit: To let down a tyre is to let the air out of it.

clue.text: Return of service wins love game

indicators.note: return means the word goes back the other way

parts.note: the RAF, Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A tennis service return wins a game to love.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis words mislead: 'service' is the RAF, turned round by 'Return of', and 'love' is O.
explanation.definitionFit: Faro is an old gambling card game, played against a banker.

clue.text: Game using four cards from the pack

explanation.definitionFit: The first is a handball court game played at English schools; the second is the four cards of value five in a deck.

clue.text: Jack Sprat would never gossip

explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme Jack Sprat could eat no fat, so he would never chomp it; the idiom also means to chat idly.

clue.text: What a gainful employment leads to

definitions.text: What a gainful employment leads to

indicators.note: leads means the leading letters, the first of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Paid work produces something.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of 'What a gainful employment' spell the answer, and pay is what such work brings.
explanation.definitionFit: A wage is the pay that a job earns.

clue.text: You once gave short measure

explanation.definitionFit: The archaic second-person pronoun; also slang for a thousandth of an inch, a tiny length.

clue.text: Vicar, about to suppress a cry of pain, produces ticket

indicators.note: to suppress means to hold down inside, so the cry goes within
about means turned round, so the title is read backwards

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is a vicar's title
ouch is what you shout when hurt

explanation.surface: A clergyman, about to stifle a yelp, hands over a ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' turns the vicar's title round to VER, and 'to suppress' holds the cry of pain inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A voucher is a slip exchangeable for goods, a kind of ticket.

clue.text: I am brought in to adorn face

indicators.note: brought in means placed inside the other piece

parts.note: to grace is to adorn or decorate
I'm is the contraction of I am

explanation.surface: Someone is hired to beautify a face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'face' is a verb sense: to pull a face.
explanation.definitionFit: To grimace is to twist the face in an expression, to pull a face.

clue.text: Old sectarian sounds despondent — you'll understand

indicators.note: sounds means the pieces are heard, not spelt

parts.note: sad means downcast, despondent; you see is said to mean you'll understand

explanation.surface: An ancient believer seems gloomy, if you follow me.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sadducees were a Jewish sect of the time of Christ, so an ancient member of a sect.

clue.text: Doesn't put out the port

indicators.note: put out means disturbed, so the letters are moved about

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to set the port wine out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' tempts as the drink; it is the Belgian ferry harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostend is a Belgian harbour town on the North Sea coast.
